boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Baton Rouge record (August 5, 1862) in Operations Against Baton Rouge [July-August 1862]. The live campaign label reads Confederate Offensive Against Baton Rouge. The destruction of the Arkansas on August 6, the evacuation of Baton Rouge on August 20 and the occupation of Port Hudson are context; multi-action totals are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 2nd Brigade, Department of the Gulf [US] and Breckinridge's Corps [CS]; the live field reads zero. Breckinridge says he left Vicksburg with somewhat less than 4,000, had no more than 3,400 on the march, 3,000 effectives by the morning report of August 4, and carried not more than 2,600 into action, besides some 200 partisan rangers; he estimated the enemy at not less than 4,500 in action (reported beforehand as not less than 5,000) and eighteen guns to his eleven. Irwin says Breckinridge reported 3,600 effective on July 30 including Ruggles, puts the Confederates in action at about 2,600 plus 400 or 500 rangers and militia, and Williams at about 2,500 fighting men with eighteen guns; Williams's troops from Vicksburg had fallen from 3,200 to about 800 effective, and Weitzel said not 1,200 could have marched five miles.
claims.rationale: Figures from an interested report and a history for different dates and bases; Breckinridge's July 30 figure differs between them. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Irwin describes the bluff at Baton Rouge as lower and more gently sloped than above, six roads leading out of the town, an unfortified Union line on an open plain with its right on the gunboats, and a dense morning fog; he calls the advantage of position slight on either side. Breckinridge says the ground was commanded by three gunboats in the river.
claims.rationale: Ground described by a history and an interested report; no map verification. The Union dispositions were Williams's, so the phase is left unresolved.

claims.value: NPS says the Confederates wished to recapture the capital. Breckinridge says he undertook to capture the garrison if the Arkansas could clear the river or divert the gunboats, and that with no more than 1,000 exhausted men around him at ten o'clock he did not pursue further. Irwin reads Van Dorn's object as regaining control of the river to Baton Rouge, and says Williams posted his left against the expected attack of the Arkansas.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from a summary, an interested report and a history.

claims.value: Breckinridge organized his force in two divisions under Clark and Ruggles; Clark pressed the attack until wounded. Irwin says Williams was killed near the close while urging his men forward, and that Cahill was entitled to the command but Dudley seems to have commanded the troops engaged for the rest of the battle; NPS says Cahill ordered a retreat to a prepared line nearer the river. The frozen commanders are Major General John C. Breckinridge and Brigadier General Thomas Williams, as on the live page.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report, a history and a summary; who directed the Union line after Williams fell is described differently. The listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory and the live result Union Victory. Breckinridge says the enemy were completely routed at the last encampment and that he withdrew for want of water and support; Irwin says it became clear to both sides that the attack had failed; NPS says the Federals finally forced the attackers to retire.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The Union evacuation on August 20 is campaign context, not this record's outcome.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 849 total (US 371; CS 478), and the live field agrees. Breckinridge gives 467 Confederate casualties; a printed footnote says the tabular statement shows only 446. Irwin gives the Confederate loss as about 84 killed, 313 wounded and 56 missing (453) and the Union loss as 84 killed, 266 wounded and 33 missing (383).
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Williams's, Butler's, Cahill's, Dudley's and the regimental reports (Nos. 5, 9, 11-23), the Union return (No. 10), Ruggles's and the other Confederate reports (Nos. 25-40), Van Dorn's report (No. 2) and the naval reports remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Richard B. Irwin's History of the Nineteenth Army Corps (Putnam's, 1892), already registered for the Red River pass, is an interested Union history by the corps' later assistant adjutant-general; its Baton Rouge chapter quotes Breckinridge's report, so it is not independent of it. Breckinridge's September 30, 1862 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XV, a shared container) is one interested Confederate family. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
